newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street clashes over U.S. Q4 growth forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street clashes over U.S. Q4 growth forecasts.

text.p: The macroeconomic question du jour on Wall Street is what will happen to the economy in the fourth quarter after it staged a substantial slowdown between July and September.
The answer? Nobody really knows.

While most analysts agree the economy has slowed with no sign of inflation, they do differ when it comes to predicting whether the slowdown marks the beginning of a long downturn or just a brief relief in a five-year expansionary cycle.
To complicate matters further, both sides can find enough evidence to support their views just by looking at the latest slew of economic data released over the last week.
Third quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP), for example, showed consumer spending rose just slightly, suggesting a faltering economy.
On the other hand, the same GDP report showed business inventories surged, hinting firms appear confident they will have enough demand for their products in the near future.
GDP data showed the economy grew by 2.2 percent in the third quarter, well below the brisk 4.7 percent increase registered in the previous quarter.
Business inventories grew to $39.6 billion in the third quarter from $7.1 billion earlier, while consumer spending slumped to post a 0.4 percent rise against 3.4 percent growth in the second quarter.

"We think fourth quarter this year will probably surprise somewhat on the upside, at least be a bit stronger than what the market and the Federal Reserve have been expecting it," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and an economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
Flanagan said a recent rally in the U.S. money market, which dragged long-term rates to the lowest levels in seven months, could reinvigorate some interest-rate sensitive sectors of the economy.

"You could be setting yourself up for a little bit stronger than expected read on growth," Flanagan added. The 30-year benchmark Treasury yield is currently around 6.65 percent, down from the year's peak at 7.20 percent in June.
But some disagreed.
"We think economic activity is waning as we're going into the fourth quarter, in line with the Fed's prediction," said Kathy Bostjancic, money market analyst at UBS Securities Inc.

Bostjancic said she believes three factors are leading the slowdown: a rise in interest rates seen in the first half of the year; a stronger dollar, which may take a toll on U.S. exports, and sluggish consumer spending due to a lack of pent-up demand.

The UBS economist said she does not believe the recent rally in the market will boost economic growth in the fourth quarter. "There is a lag factor there that has to be taken into account," Bostjancic said.
But there is one thing going forward that all analysts seem to agree on. Consumers are the wild card in the fourth quarter and wherever they go, the economy will follow.
Analysts said some recent indicators suggest Americans appear to be willing to spend a fair amount during the upcoming holiday shopping season.
Economists said the employment rate still remains firm (October non-farm payrolls grew by 210,000 jobs), wages are steady at higher levels and consumer confidence indicators remain relatively high.
"All these are ingredients that bode well for the holiday shopping season," Dean Witter's Flanagan said.
Thus analysts said income and spending data for September hinted consumers are accumulating some wealth that could be spent sooner rather than later.
Personal income data for September rose 0.6 percent, while spending grew a meager 0.1 percent.

"We saw another good increase in income... but it looks like people are either buying stocks with their extra income or they're paying down some of their debt," said Paul Kasriel, senior economist at Northern Trust Co.
Some analysts said, however, that a lack of pent-up demand in the economy after five years of growth may keep consumers at bay.
"Pent-up demand has been largely exhausted...even if interest rates are lower, it's not going to entice consumers to go out and purchase the same items they just did," UBS's Bostjancic said.
Analysts' estimates for fourth quarter GDP growth range from 1.2 percent to 2.5 percent.
